t: LeetCode 3465 — Find Products with Valid Serial Numbers
o: We must return every product whose `description` contains a substring of the exact form `SN` + 4 digits + `-` + 4 digits, where the serial is embedded anywhere in the text. The key subtlety is the word "exactly": row 3 contains `SN1234-56789`, which must be rejected because the group after the hyphen has 5 digits. So a naive search for `SN\d{4}-\d{4}` would wrongly match its first 10 characters. We therefore need boundary checks ensuring no extra digit directly follows the matched tail (and, defensively, none directly precedes the `SN`). Since this is a pure string-pattern filter over rows, regular expressions are the natural tool, and the result is ordered by `product_id` ascending.
k: The pattern is fixed-shape: literal `SN`, then 4 digits, `-`, then 4 digits — perfect for a regex.
"Exactly" means we must guard against longer digit runs: reject when another digit follows the last digit (e.g. `SN1234-56789`).
A single filtered SELECT with REGEXP solves it; ordering by product_id finishes the job.

a.n: Approach 1: Regex match with digit-boundary guards
a.i: Use one regex that captures the whole valid shape and asserts digit boundaries on both sides. In SQL, `REGEXP` (MySQL 8 / ICU) supports lookarounds, so we can write `(?<![0-9])SN[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{4}(?![0-9])`. The trailing negative lookahead is what eliminates `SN1234-56789`; the leading lookbehind prevents matches like `1SN1234-5678` where the leading digits run continues. The same logic ports to every language via their native regex engines.
s: Build the pattern: optional non-digit start boundary, literal `SN`, `[0-9]{4}`, `-`, `[0-9]{4}`, end boundary forbidding a following digit.
Filter rows whose description matches the pattern.
Return all columns ordered by product_id ascending.
a.t: O(n · m) — each of the n descriptions of length m is scanned once by the regex engine.
a.sp: O(n) — output storage; the regex itself is constant size.

a.n: Approach 2: Pure SQL solution (the intended Database answer)
a.i: On LeetCode this problem is answered with a single SQL query. MySQL 8's ICU regex engine accepts lookbehind/lookahead, so the same guarded pattern works directly in `REGEXP`. If lookarounds are unavailable (older engines), an equivalent trick is requiring the character after the second digit group to be a non-digit or end-of-string via alternation.
s: Write the guarded regex as a string literal.
Use it inside WHERE ... REGEXP to keep only valid descriptions.

c.python:
# Intended solution language is SQL:
# SELECT * FROM products
# WHERE description REGEXP '(?<![0-9])SN[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{4}(?![0-9])'
# ORDER BY product_id;

a.t: O(n · m) — one regex scan per row.

w: In an interview (or on LeetCode), submit the single-line SQL query from Approach 2 — it is the canonical answer for a Database-tagged Easy. The main pitfall is forgetting the "exactly" constraint: without the trailing `(?!\d)` guard, `SN1234-56789` passes incorrectly. A secondary edge case is a serial glued to preceding digits (`9SN1234-5678`); the leading guard handles it, though many accepted solutions omit it since tests may not cover it. Case sensitivity matters too: `sn1234-5678` must not match, so avoid case-insensitive flags. Likely follow-ups: extract the serial itself with `REGEXP_SUBSTR`, count valid serials per row, or handle multiple serials per description.
